summary:
Colombia's formal legal framework is among the most developed in Latin America. Since a rule change approved in June 2015, trans Colombians change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments; the official Reyes, who defended the change, described those examinations as "profoundly invasive of privacy rights... rooted in unacceptable prejudice". Constitutional Court jurisprudence dating from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition on the basis of self-recognition without a surgical requirement, and national identification documents have carried "trans" and "non-binary" markers since November 2025.

That framework sits alongside lethal, targeted violence. On 5 April 2025 a 28-second video went viral showing Sara Millerey, 32, flailing in a creek in Bello, Antioquia, near Medellín, unable to swim with fractured legs, arms and hands, before she drowned. Her mother, Sandra Borja, said: "They killed her for being who she was." President Petro ordered an urgent investigation, and solidarity events were held in several cities.

Killings of queer Colombians continued after the Millerey case. In Guajira, armed groups have posted flyers, from March 2024, carrying a kill list of named individuals and stating that all will be military targets, expressly including trans people. In Caquetá, flyer campaigns announce a "social cleansing" of "drug addicts, prostitutes and faggots"; a trans salon owner, Tatiana Cespedes, was forced to move twice after death threats from armed men, trans women in the department have few economic options beyond sex work, and a friend of interviewee Yesenia Rodríguez was killed. Reporting frames these repeated killings as calculated brutality persisting through the country's decades-long armed conflict.

The recorded tolls are raw counts without population denominators and cannot be read as a per-capita risk rate: more than 40 transgender women were killed in Colombia in 2023; the Attorney General's Office recorded 35 LGBTI murders from January to May 2025; 13 trans people were killed in the first quarter of 2025.

Colombian institutions have treated parts of this violence as conflict-driven persecution. In July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, the state acknowledging that conflict-driven violence amounted to gender persecution, a crime against humanity; the UN Human Rights Committee noted concern. The UN Independent Expert on SOGI violence and discrimination, Graeme Reid, concluded a fact-finding mission across multiple Colombian cities in May 2025, praising the government's legal reforms and commitment to equality while warning of a stark disconnect between institutional progress and daily lived experience, with widespread discrimination and violence to be urgently addressed as killings rise.

Access to public and commercial facilities has been protected by court order, including judgment T-314 of 2011 on the Tequendama Hotel's refusal of access, judgment T-909 of 2011 ordering Cosmocentro mall guards in Cali to be trained so as not to repress public affection, and judgment T-301 of 2004 ordering Santa Marta police to stop harassing people at the city boardwalk. In custody, a 2011 Constitutional Court ruling allowed a transgender woman prisoner to choose her own hairstyle and makeup, and a Colombian court has since issued a ruling protecting the rights of a trans woman deprived of liberty.

In care, the 2016 government decree specifically addresses LGBTI rights in health care, and the 2016 report Cartografía de derechos trans in Colombia, by OutRight Action International, El Aquelarre Trans and PAIIS at Universidad de los Andes, recommended ending psychiatric pathologization of transgender identity and abandoning sterilisation as a prerequisite for other physical changes. Conversion therapy bans remain unpassed as of 2025.

On partner recognition, same-sex marriage has been available since 2016 and adoption since 2015. The first same-sex marriage conducted abroad was registered in March 2016, and the National Registry issued a memo ordering all notaries and registrars to register same-sex marriages performed outside the country; couples presenting a stamped marriage certificate and identification papers at the nearest designated office are entitled to the same visa, healthcare benefits, inheritance and pension rights as other spouses. A trans visitor whose marriage would be read as same-sex under the sex marker on their documents is therefore recognised in the same terms.
tangentialFactors:
Colombian society remains generally conservative despite supportive media coverage, including gay characters in prime-time programmes such as Dr Mata and a lesbian scene in A corazón abierto. A bloc of conservative senators defeated the civil union bill in Congress on 19 June 2007, and the country's Inspector General asked the Constitutional Court in 2015 to invalidate all same-sex marriages approved in Colombia.

Organised opposition to the recognition framework has been substantial but has not reversed it. By 31 March 2016 a campaign to force a referendum repealing the November 2015 same-sex adoption ruling had gathered 1.8 million signatures including 45 members of Congress, and a congressional committee shelved it 20 to 12 in May 2017. An Invamer poll of October 2019 put same-sex marriage support at 50% against 47% opposed and adoption at 36% in favour against 62% opposed, while 2016 polls showed 37% to 40% support for marriage and only 22% for adoption.

Conversion therapy bans remain unpassed: the Inconvertibles bill of Congressperson Mauricio Toro, introduced 10 May 2022, had failed by 2024, and Congressperson Carolina Giraldo proposed the similar bill Quiérele siempre in 2025.

The Constitutional Court has repeatedly protected public expression of same-sex affection: in 1994 it disapproved the National Council of Television's refusal to air a commercial featuring a same-sex couple; judgment T-268 of 2000 permitted a pride parade the Mayor of Neiva had blocked; judgment T-301 of 2004 ordered Santa Marta police to stop harassment at the boardwalk; judgment T-314 of 2011 held a hotel's refusal of access as discriminatory; and judgment T-909 of 2011 ordered mall guards in Cali to take a course so as not to repress public affection. As of 2020 military culture still discouraged discussion of same-sex attraction under a "se puede ser, pero no demostrar" norm.

The comparison the sources draw is between formal protection and lived exposure: strong statutory protections alongside documented killing, which is the gap the UN Independent Expert's May 2025 mission was convened to address.
localsOnly:
Residents change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, a route open since June 2015 without medical examination; Constitutional Court jurisprudence from 1993 grounds recognition in self-recognition rather than surgery, and national identification documents have carried "trans" and "non-binary" markers since November 2025.

Law passed in 2011 penalises discrimination based on sexual orientation with one to three years' imprisonment plus fines. Following the August 2014 suicide of student Sergio Urrego after discrimination by his teachers, the Constitutional Court ruled for his family and ordered the Ministry of Education to review, within a year, the coexistence manuals of all schools nationwide so that no article discriminates against children by sexual orientation or gender identity; in 1998 the Court had already ruled that public school teachers cannot be fired for revealing their sexual orientation and that private religious schools cannot ban gay students from enrolling.

The 2016 Ministry of Interior presidential decree set procedural obligations for government institutions covering LGBTI rights in public education, health care, prisons and as victims of armed conflict, and a May 2018 executive decree by President Juan Manuel Santos extended guarantees to housing, work, recreation, sports and culture. The 2016 government decree specifically addresses LGBTI rights in health care.

Family and partnership rights for residents: since 2014 LGBTQ individuals can adopt their partner's biological child, the 4 November 2015 ruling granted full same-sex adoption rights barring agency discrimination, and a 12 November 2015 ruling required birth registration listing two mothers or two fathers. The Constitutional Court extended social security (health insurance) benefits to same-sex couples on 5 October 2007 and pension rights on 17 April 2008, so such couples now enjoy the main benefits other couples have on the same terms.

In custody, a 2011 Constitutional Court ruling allowed a transgender woman prisoner to choose her own hairstyle and makeup, and a further court ruling addressed the treatment of a trans woman deprived of liberty. The 2016 report Cartografía de derechos trans in Colombia recommended ending psychiatric pathologization of transgender identity and abandoning sterilisation as a prerequisite for other physical changes; conversion therapy bans remain unpassed as of 2025.

Bogotá and Medellín have established gay neighbourhoods, bars, and counselling and legal advice centres. In 2012 the Constitutional Court found that sexual orientation cannot be a criterion for preventing blood donation and ordered the Ministry of Health and Social Protection to rewrite donation regulations so that they assess risk by sexual behaviour rather than orientation.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory addresses entry, visa or border screening of trans travellers, airport or land-border treatment of gender-nonconforming presentation, or document-marker flagging on arrival. That layer is unresolved here and is not sourced either way.

Whether the "trans" and "non-binary" markers carried on national identification documents since November 2025 are reproduced on passports, or recognised by foreign authorities, is not sourced.

The Ambito Jurídico report on the ruling protecting the rights of a trans woman deprived of liberty does not specify the deciding court, the date, or the operative holding; only the existence of a ruling on the treatment of trans detainees is established.

The killing figures available (more than 40 transgender women in 2023; 35 LGBTI murders recorded by the Attorney General's Office from January to May 2025; 13 trans people killed in the first quarter of 2025) are raw counts with no population denominator and no comparison to the national homicide rate, so they cannot be converted into a comparative risk rate.

The status of a conversion therapy ban is unresolved: the Inconvertibles bill had failed by 2024 and the Quiérele siempre bill was proposed in 2025, with no sourced outcome for either.

Regional variation is documented only for the provinces named in the sources (Antioquia, Guajira, Caquetá); enforcement practice elsewhere in the country is not sourced.
